definition: PingOne's own MCP endpoint, run by Ping, for the Management API admin plane. This app connects to it as a client, lists its tools and calls them. An administrator signs in to it (a user sign-in, not a worker token); the tools listed follow that user's admin roles. Endpoint shape: https://mcp.pingone.{region}/admin/{envId}/mcp (Ping's MCP docs; the api.pingone shape from the pingone-mcp skill is UNVERIFIED).
The part of PingOne that manages PingOne itself: applications, populations, users, DaVinci flows, environment configuration. It is not your own product's data or end-user tools.

A PingOne application with admin roles, used by unattended callers such as scripts and services. Give it only the roles the caller needs: an overprivileged worker is as risky as an overprivileged REST credential. In this lab only the Setup card uses one, against the Management API, to create the sign-in application. The hosted PingOne MCP server does not take a worker's token: it takes an administrator's own sign-in.

The OAuth grant a worker application uses: it presents its own client id and secret at the token endpoint and gets a bearer token. The secret is only ever sent to the token endpoint. In this lab it is used only by Setup, for one Management API token; the MCP server is called with a signed-in user's token.

The interactive sign-in, as PingOne's native flow (pi.flow): this app shows the sign-in form itself, drives the flow at the authorization server, and gets a code that it exchanges using a one-time secret (the PKCE verifier, S256) as a public client. There is no redirect and no callback. This app adds a nonce, names the MCP server as the resource (RFC 8707), and checks the id token's signature, issuer and audience.

The server lists only the tools the signed-in user's admin roles allow. A short list usually means missing roles, not a broken server (Ping's MCP docs; pingone-mcp skill). The same URL shows different tools to a viewer and an admin: in the mock, mock.viewer and mock.admin.

Prefer the hosted MCP tools for application, population and user reads, user management and DaVinci reads; fall back to the Management API for what MCP does not cover, and on any MCP failure do not retry in a loop (pingone-mcp skill).
Every tool is classed read, write or destructive. Write and destructive calls are blocked until the operator turns on allow writes for that connection. Unknown tools count as write.

Even with writes allowed, a write call is refused until the request carries confirm:true and the hash of the exact arguments that were shown. Destructive calls also need the tool name typed. Change one argument and the hash no longer matches.

A local, append-only record of every call, allowed or blocked: when, which connection, which tool, its class, the outcome, the arguments exactly as sent, and their hash. This app's own stored secrets and tokens are masked if they appear as a value.
